Argument.summary: The birth rate will decrease due to COVID-19 because of marriage postponement, income reduction among young and low-income groups, and childcare difficulties.

c1.text: The birth rate will decrease due to COVID-19.

c2.text: Strong social distancing and restrictions on public facilities and travel led many people to postpone or give up on marriage.

c3.text: Especially among low-income groups and young people, unemployment rates rose and income decreased, increasing economic hardship.

c4.text: Because the economic burden of childbirth and childrearing is high, a decrease in income will result in a decrease in births.

c5.text: Remote work stress and the closure or partial operation of childcare facilities made raising children even more difficult.

c6.text: Due to childcare and childrearing challenges, families with or without children are likely to postpone or give up on having children.

h1.text: The total number of infants and young children decreased from July 2019 to July 2022.

h2.text: There was no difference in the population under one year old from July 2019 to July 2022.

h3.text: A lack of difference in the population under one year old indicates little change in the birth rate, so a decrease in total infants does not mean a fall in the birth rate.

a.note: The tempting inference ra1 (decrease in infants implies decrease in birth rate) is undercut by h3: no difference in the under-one population indicates little change in births.

h4.text: Per capita GDP in 2019 was 31,929,000 KRW and in 2020 was 31,637,000 KRW, showing little difference.

h5.text: Incomes among low-income groups and young people did not decrease.

h6.text: Per capita GDP can remain unchanged even if low-income and young people's incomes decrease, provided middle or upper income groups' incomes increase.

b.note: The tempting inference rb1 (stable per capita GDP implies youth and low-income incomes did not drop) is undercut by h6: per capita GDP can remain unchanged if higher-income groups earn more.

h7.text: In August 2019 and August 2021, the percentage of economically active and inactive women who reported being currently pregnant was 10% for both groups, showing almost no change.

h8.text: Families did not postpone or give up on having children due to childcare and childrearing challenges.

c.note: The stable pregnancy rate supports h8, which is contrary to c6, undermining the childcare ground of the argument.
